Terraform user of a couple of years managing dev/qa/prod infra: aside from minor HCL changes, they've had no major problems keeping up with new versions. Being able to rebuild everything (Kubernetes, DNS, MySQL, etc.) automatically has 'saved us more than once.'

"I hate Terraform with a passion but it is probably the best tool out there for managing cloud infrastructure." Biggest downsides: an 'awful half-baked language', awkward modules and value passing, and static providers. For example, you can't create a Kubernetes cluster and then add a resource to it in one stack. Performance is so bad you need to split stacks anyway.

The biggest problem is that the state file is a JSON blob whose hierarchy directly maps your code structure. This makes refactoring a nightmare, since you keep having to fudge the state file or map code resources to state resources.

Workaround for refactoring: use 'terraform state mv'. After the first handful of moves it feels almost as natural as refactoring modules in any codebase. If it's a big mess, you can 'rm' and 'import'.

Merging multiple modules with hundreds or thousands of resources each into an array of modules via state mv is a big job. Big refactorings are particularly hard in TF because resource referencing is rigid. Doing this in Chef is much simpler, since resource name and address match and are under the developer's control.
Workaround: one user habitually backs up the state file by hand before changes (aws s3 cp of terraform.tfstate to a .bak file). Another suggested S3 automatic object versioning for the same purpose.

With the Kubernetes and Helm providers, one user has had to do applies in multiple steps when creating the cluster in the same run. Another said a similar single-run setup works but doesn't handle cluster deletion well.

For a cross-account AWS task (an ACM certificate in one account, Route53 DNS in another), CDK and CloudFormation couldn't do it in one step without horrific hacks, but "with Terraform it's absolutely trivial." The user abandoned CDK and came back to 'my old friend Terraform.'

Loves HCL for infrastructure and doesn't want a real programming language, but lists pain points:
- Remote state as a data source leaves infra broken until a second apply.
- Public modules are 'absolute garbage', with more input complexity than the resources they wrap.
- A clean 'apply' can still cause an outage mid-execution.

Complaints at v1.0:
- Still no dynamic providers, causing copypasta when creating Kubernetes clusters.
- Secrets are stored unencrypted in state.
- No phased workspaces even in commercial products.
- Sensitive variables can't be overridden when importing in Terraform Cloud/Enterprise.
Long-time user since before 0.12: the workflow, meaningful diffs and reproducible infrastructure-as-code were 'a massive step up' from cloud console and CI scripts.
Much of the hate targets pre-0.12 HCL1. With for_each and dynamic blocks you can nearly ditch variable files and local modules and add infrastructure by editing a local YAML file.
"After i was introduced to Pulumi, i felt at home ... there is no going back to Terraform."
"You people hating on Terraform are spoiled. My company insists on using CloudFormation, which I hate with a passion."
A user who looked into Terraform was disappointed that it didn't abstract away cloud providers. You still have to target and code against each provider specifically and know its terminology.

Small annoyance: there's no graceful way to set up a new module with backend state from the start. You must create resources with local state first, then re-run terraform init after adding the backend block.

Pull requests for much-wanted features, with working documentation and passing integration tests, often took months to a year to be accepted and merged. The user felt HashiCorp engineers were incentivized to work on features tied to paid services.

Impressed by recent declarative handling of imperative actions such as import and state moves. These used to require very careful coordination in large active configurations and are now 'quite simple and safe.'

On the BUSL change: the 'competitive offering' wording is seen as vague. Example: if you built a popular cost-estimation tool like infracost and Terraform Cloud later added that feature, would you be out of business?
At launch: decent coverage of AWS resources, but ElastiCache and CloudWatch were missing. Without CloudWatch, the user wasn't sure how to set up a useful autoscaling group.
